extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent practitioners and applicants (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining, applying, and overcoming rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 (printed publication/patent, public use, on-sale, foreign patent bars, and application-publication prior art), including rules for effective filing dates and when to rely on abstracts or full-text references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on abstracts versus underlying full-text documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abstract is used to support a rejection, the evidence relied upon is the facts contained in the abstract, not additional facts that may be contained in the underlying full text document. Citation of and reliance upon an abstract without citation of and reliance upon the underlying scientific document is generally inappropriate where both the abstract and the underlying document are prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A copy of the underlying document must be obtained and analyzed to determine whether both qualify as prior art. If the underlying document is not in English and the examiner seeks to rely on it, a translation must be obtained so the record is clear as to the precise facts relied upon. The record must state whether the examiner is relying upon the abstract or the full text. Rationale: the full text may fully anticipate or teach away from the invention, and the abstract may have a different effective publication date. Normally the underlying document should be used when both qualify; in limited circumstances a non-final rejection may rely on the abstract alone but the full text (and translation, if needed) should be supplied in the next Office action. See Ex parte Jones; see MPEP §706.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions in the specification or prosecution can be relied on as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission which can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify as prior art under the statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Riverwood Int’l Corp. v. R.A. Jones & Co., Constant v. Advanced Micro-Devices, and MPEP §2129. Where the admitted prior art anticipates the claim but does not qualify as prior art under any paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102, the claim may nonetheless be rejected as being anticipated by the admitted prior art without citing to 35 U.S.C. 102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty) and 103 (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: For anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention either explicitly or impliedly; any feature not directly taught must be inherently present. For a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference teachings must be modified in a way which would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the legal distinction in mind when formulating rejections; see MPEP §§2131–2146 for guidance on patentability determinations under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the effective filing date of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date of a U.S. application may be determined as follows: (A) continuation/divisional with requirements of 35 U.S.C. 120 and 365(c) satisfied -> effective filing date is the earliest filing date in the line; (B) continuation-in-part -> claims not supported by parent have the new application's filing date, claims fully supported have parent's effective date; (C) claiming foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) or 365(a)/(b) -> effective filing date is the U.S. filing date unless (A) or (B) apply (foreign priority document filing date is not the effective filing date though it may be used as references); (D) claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a provisional -> effective filing date is the provisional filing date for claims fully supported under 35 U.S.C.112 first paragraph by the provisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§706.02, 1893.03(b), 201.11, 1895, 1895.01, and 1896 for additional information on continuations, divisionals, CIPs, internationals entering national stage, and claiming benefit/priority; ensure enablement and written description requirements are met for benefit claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding whether to apply 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an examiner finds a printed publication or patent that discloses the claimed invention, the examiner should determine whether the rejection should be made under 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e) by determining the effective filing date of the application and comparing it with the date of the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP §706.02 for methods of determining effective filing date and comparison; determining the correct subsection affects statutory bar and available responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (statutory bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication or issue date of the reference that is more than one year prior to the effective filing date of the application qualifies the reference as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (statutory bar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the last day of the year dated from the date of publication falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or Federal holiday, the publication is not a statutory bar if the application was filed on the next succeeding business day (Ex parte Olah). Changes to 37 CFR 1.6(a)(2) and 1.10 regarding Express Mail filing dates do not affect applicant’s right to defer filing to the next business day when the 1-year grace period expires on a weekend/holiday. See MPEP §706.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the issue or publication date of references
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must determine the issue or publication date of the reference so that a proper comparison between the application and reference dates can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A magazine is effective as a printed publication under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as of the date it reached the addressee and not the date it was placed in the mail; see Protein Foundation Inc. v. Brenner and MPEP §707.05(f). For foreign patents see MPEP §901.05. See also MPEP §§2124, 2126, and 2128–2128.02 for case law relevant to reference date determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(e) inventive entity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to apply a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the inventive entity of the application must be different than that of the reference. Where there are joint inventors, only one inventor needs to be different for the inventive entities to be different and a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) is applicable even if there are some inventors in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (AIPA and later amendments) applies in examination of all applications and reexaminations; see MPEP §706.02(f)(1) for guidelines on applying 102(e). Be mindful of retroactivity and special handling of international applications filed prior to November 29, 2000.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for international applications and 35 U.S.C. 102(e) dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Under revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e), an international filing date which is on or after November 29, 2000 is a United States filing date for prior art purposes if the international application (a) designated the United States, and (b) was published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in the English language. If those three conditions are met, the international filing date (or an earlier U.S. filing date properly claimed) may be the prior art date for the reference under 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International applications filed prior to November 29, 2000 are subject to the pre-AIPA version of 102(e) and may not reach back via international filing dates; publications of international applications filed before Nov 29, 2000 do not have a 102(e) date (but may be prior art under 102(a) or (b)). See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) and 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/374 descriptions for details and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(b) can be overcome by: (A) persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; (C) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78(a) (by amending the specification or filing an application data sheet) and establishing the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112 enablement/written description; or (D) perfecting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) by complying with 37 CFR 1.78(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a benefit claim under 119(e) is perfected, the rejection must be reconsidered to determine whether the prior art still qualifies under 102(b) or instead qualifies under 102(a). See MPEP §706.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentable distinction; (B) amending claims; (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing prior invention if the reference is not a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claiming the same patentable invention; (E) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); or (F) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 (with required enablement/written description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the claims of the reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication and the application are directed to the same invention or are obvious variants, a 1.131 affidavit is not an acceptable method of overcoming the rejection; examiner must determine whether double patenting or an interference is appropriate. See MPEP §715, §716.10, §804, and Chapter 2300 for interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(a) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentable distinction; (B) amending claims; (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing prior invention if the reference is not a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claiming the same patentable invention; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (E) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); or (F) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 1.131 affidavit is inappropriate when the reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claims the same invention or obvious variants (see 37 CFR 41.203(a) and MPEP §715). See MPEP §706.02 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use or on-sale determinations (35 U.S.C. 102(a)/(b)) and information requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If evidence indicates the invention was sold by applicant or known by others in this country, the examiner must determine if 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(b) applies. If the evidence points to knowledge within the year prior to effective filing date then 102(a) applies; if activity occurred more than one year prior then 102(b) applies. No 102(a) rejection should be made if applicant made the invention and only disclosed it to others within the year prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To resolve public use or on-sale issues the examiner may require applicant to answer specific questions and explain or supplement any evidence of record under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.104(a)(2). Information sought should be restricted to that reasonably necessary; examiner may make a requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 where reasonably necessary. A one- or two-month time period should be set for reply to the requirement unless part of an Office action having a shortened statutory period; failure to reply will result in abandonment (35 U.S.C. 133). If insufficient information exists, make a requirement for more information; use form paragraph 7.104 or 7.16 when a prima facie case exists. See MPEP §2133.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraph 7.104 / requirement for information when public use/on sale is raised
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶7.104 Requirement for Information: An issue of public use or on sale activity has been raised in this application. In order for the examiner to properly consider patentability of the claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. 102(b), additional information regarding this issue is required as follows: [1] Applicant is reminded that failure to fully reply to this requirement for information will result in a holding of abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner note: information sought should be restricted to what is reasonably necessary; set one- or two-month reply period unless SSP; if sufficient evidence exists to establish a prima facie case of public use/on sale, use form paragraph 7.16 to make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(b). See MPEP §2133.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) (abandonment of the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 102(c), abandonment of the 'invention' (as distinguished from abandonment of an application) results in loss of right to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2134 for case law clarifying criteria for abandonment under 35 U.S.C. 102(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — four conditions for foreign-patent statutory bar
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 102(d) establishes four conditions which, if all present, establish a statutory bar against granting a patent in this country: (A) the foreign application must be filed more than 12 months before the effective filing date of the U.S. application; (B) the foreign and U.S. applications must be filed by the same applicant, legal representatives or assigns; (C) the foreign application must have actually issued as a patent or inventor’s certificate before the filing in the United States (need not be published but rights must be enforceable); (D) the same invention must be involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a foreign patent or inventor’s certificate is discovered, the rejection is made under 35 U.S.C. 102(d) on the ground of statutory bar. See MPEP §2135.01 for case law clarifying each requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search guidance for 35 U.S.C. 102(d) prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should only undertake a search for an issued foreign patent for use as 35 U.S.C. 102(d) prior art if there is a reasonable possibility that a foreign patent covering the same subject matter has been granted to the same inventive entity before the U.S. effective filing date (i.e., time between foreign and U.S. filings is greater than the usual time it takes for a patent to issue in that foreign country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal probability of foreign patent issuing before U.S. filing is often slight; pendency varies by country (e.g., Belgium may grant in a month; Japan may take several years). Search may be accomplished on electronic databases by the examiner or Scientific and Technical Information Center staff (see MPEP §901.06(a)). The document must be a patent or inventor’s certificate and not merely a published/laid-open application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines / flow for determining the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for a potential reference
rubrics_metrics.description: I. Determine the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for each potential reference by following: (A) the potential reference must be a U.S. patent, a U.S. application publication (35 U.S.C.122(b)), or a WIPO publication of an international application under PCT Article 21(2); (B) determine if the potential reference resulted from, or claimed the benefit of, an international application; (C) if it did, determine whether the international application meets three conditions (filed on/after Nov 29, 2000; designated the U.S.; published under PCT Art.21(2) in English) — if so the international filing date is a U.S. filing date for 102(e) purposes; if not, follow subrules (C)(2)-(4) for various situations; (D) foreign application filing dates claimed in publications/patents may not be used as 102(e) dates for prior art purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed steps: (A) if reference did not result from or claim benefit of an international application, its 102(e) date is its earliest effective U.S. filing date (consider proper benefit claims 119(e)/120 and 112 support). (C)(1)-(4) and (D) enumerate how to treat international applications filed before/after Nov 29, 2000, publications, U.S. patents issued from internationals, and earlier filing dates properly claimed. See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) for flowcharts, examples and nine illustrative examples covering common factual situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples to determine prior art dates under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nine examples are presented to illustrate the prior art dates of U.S. and WIPO publications of patent applications and U.S. patents under 35 U.S.C. 102(e); the examples cover common factual situations encountered when determining the 102(e) date of a reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult these examples and timelines to understand histories of references (e.g., U.S. application publications, patents, priority claims, international applications) and to determine applicable prior art dates when applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e). See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) and accompanying flow charts.
